en: The Questions of King Milinda,
Chapter on Nibbāna,
Section 5: The Question on the Performance of Exertion
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
'How might this suffering cease, and how might other suffering not arise?'"
“Great King, this is the purpose of our going forth.
“What is the use of striving beforehand? Should one not strive when the time has actually arrived?
The Elder replied:
“Great King, when the time has already arrived, effort is of no use; effort is effective only when applied beforehand.
“Give me an illustration.
“What do you think, Great King? When you are thirsty, would you then have a well dug or a pond excavated, thinking, ‘I shall drink water’?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, when the time has already arrived, effort is of no use; rather, effort is effective only when applied beforehand.
“Give me a further illustration.”
“What do you think, great king? When you are hungry, would you then have a field plowed, rice sown, and grain harvested, thinking, ‘I shall eat a meal’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“In the same way, great king, when the time has already arrived, effort is ineffective; it is only when one exerts effort beforehand that it becomes effective.”
“Give me another simile.
“What do you think, Great King? When a battle is imminent for you, would you have a moat dug, a rampart built, a gate-tower built, a watchtower built, and grain [stored]?”
“If you were to have someone bring it to you, would you then train in elephant-riding,
train in horsemanship, train in charioteering, train in archery, and train in swordsmanship?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“In the same way, great king, effort made when the time has already arrived is ineffective; effort made beforehand is what accomplishes the task.
For this was said, great king, by the Blessed One:
‘One should do that beforehand…’”
Whatever one knows to be for one's own welfare,
a wise person, mindful, should exert effort, and not according to the thinking of a cartwright.
Just as a cartwright,
having abandoned a smooth, level highway,
ascends a rugged, uneven path;
He meditates like one whose axle is broken.
Thus, having departed from the Dhamma and followed what is not the Dhamma;
“Foolish, having entered the jaws of Death,
he sits brooding like one whose axle is broken. “You are skillful,
venerable Nāgasena,” [the king said].
The fifth question: On the performance of effort.
